literal: For merit his fief was increased by eight hundred households, and he was advanced in title to General Who Pacifies the West.
idiomatic: Merit added eight hundred households to his fief and raised him to general who pacifies the west.

literal: He was also dismissed to Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, with bearer of the staff, mobile secretariat, and command as before.
idiomatic: He was also named right vice director of the Masters of Writing, keeping bearer of the staff, mobile secretariat, and command unchanged.

literal: Soon he was transferred to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry and Grand Master with ritual parity to the Three Excellencies; the rest as before.
idiomatic: Shortly he became grand general of chariots and cavalry and grand master with ritual parity to the three excellencies, other posts unchanged.

literal: It happened that Xiao Baoyin and others suffered great defeat at Pingliang; Hao too fled back to the capital.
idiomatic: When Xiao Baoyin and others were routed at Pingliang, Hao also fled to the capital.

literal: At that time Ge Rong advanced south and gradually pressed on Ye.
idiomatic: Ge Rong was then pushing south, drawing ever nearer to Ye.

literal: At the beginning of Wutai, Hao was made Attendant-in-Ordinary, General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Master Who Opens a Headquarters with ritual parity to the Three Excellencies, and Inspector of Xiang Province to resist Rong.
idiomatic: Early in Wutai he was made attendant-in-ordinary, general of agile cavalry, grand master who opens a headquarters with three-offices parity, and Xiang inspector to hold off Rong.

literal: When Hao reached Ji commandery, Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang and installed Emperor Zhuang; an edict appointed Hao Grand Preceptor, with headquarters, attendant, inspector, and princedom all as before.
idiomatic: Hao had reached Ji when Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang and enthroned Zhuangdi; an edict kept him grand preceptor with his headquarters, attendant post, inspector title, and princedom unchanged.

literal: Hao, because Ge Rong invaded south and Erzhu committed outrage, then lingered and looked about, plotting a policy to secure himself.
idiomatic: With Ge Rong pressing south and Erzhu Rong's violence abroad, Hao hesitated and cast about for a way to save himself.

literal: Earlier Hao had memorialized his maternal uncle Fan Zun as Inspector of Yin Province; Zun, because Ge Rong filled and pressed the region, could not take up the post.
idiomatic: He had earlier asked that his uncle Fan Zun be made Yin inspector, but Ge Rong's occupation kept Zun from taking office.

literal: Hao ordered Zun to halt provisionally at Ye.
idiomatic: Hao had Zun hold temporarily at Ye.

literal: Hao, already harboring a divergent plot, then sent Zun to act in Xiang Province affairs in place of the former inspector Li Shen, as inner and outer support for himself.
idiomatic: Once he nursed a separate design, he sent Zun to run Xiang in place of the former inspector Li Shen, making him support within and without.

literal: The Xiang Province mobile secretariat Zhen Mi had earlier received the court's order, [18] entrusting him to guard Ye.
idiomatic: Zhen Mi of the Xiang mobile secretariat had already been ordered [18] to hold Ye.

literal: Learning of Hao's divergent plot and fearing Zun would make trouble, they jointly deposed Zun, returned and installed Li Shen to act in provincial affairs, and then sent troops to watch Hao's course of loyalty or rebellion.
idiomatic: Seeing Hao's disloyal intent and fearing Zun would rebel, they deposed Zun together, put Li Shen back in charge of the province, and sent troops to test whether Hao would submit or revolt.

literal: Hao with several thousand men won in battle wherever he turned, held the capital region, issued orders on his own authority, and popular sentiment everywhere looked to his governance.
idiomatic: With a few thousand men he won wherever he fought, held the capital, ruled by his own orders, and the realm looked to his rule with hope.

literal: Yet he deemed himself heaven's appointee and grew quite proud and slack.
idiomatic: He took heaven's mandate for granted and turned arrogant and lax.

literal: Guests and intimates of long standing were all shown favor; they interfered in government affairs, and day and night he drank heavily, heedless of army and state.
idiomatic: Old clients and favorites were indulged, meddled in policy, and he drank day and night without heed for war or rule.

literal: The southern troops under his command plundered the market wards.
idiomatic: His southern soldiers preyed on the markets.

literal: Court and countryside alike were disappointed.
idiomatic: Court and country alike lost heart.

literal: At the time there was also harsh exaction; public and private were unsettled.
idiomatic: Harsh levies meanwhile left public and private life insecure.

literal: Emperor Zhuang and Erzhu Rong returned their army to campaign against Hao.
idiomatic: Zhuangdi and Erzhu Rong marched back to crush Hao.

literal: From resistance at Heqiao they fought; the imperial army crossed at Mazhu ford; Guanshou was defeated in battle and captured, and defeat followed in succession.
idiomatic: They fought at Heqiao; the imperial host crossed at Mazhu; Guanshou was beaten and taken, and defeat cascaded.

literal: Hao led several hundred horsemen of his personal guard and stalwart southern troops, and came out through Huanyuan Pass.
idiomatic: Hao fled with a few hundred household guards and picked southern fighters through Huanyuan Pass.

literal: At Linying, Hao's mounted followers scattered, and he was beheaded by a Linying county soldier.
idiomatic: Near Linying his escort broke up and a county soldier cut off his head.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously given bearer of the staff, Attendant-in-Ordinary, controller of all military affairs of Ji, Ding, Xiang, and Yin provinces, General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Marshal, and Inspector of Ji Province.
idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne he was posthumously made bearer of the staff, attendant-in-ordinary, commander of Ji, Ding, Xiang, and Yin armies, general of agile cavalry, grand marshal, and Ji inspector.

literal: In the Wuding era his son Suoluo inherited.
idiomatic: In Wuding his son Suoluo succeeded.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, enfeoffments were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi's founding the rank was lowered by rule.

literal: Hao's younger brother Xu, [19] courtesy name Baoyi.
idiomatic: Hao's younger brother Xu, [19] styled Baoyi.

literal: He began his career as Regular Attendant, was transferred to Secretariat Gentleman, and served as Guard General, Vice Director of the Household Guard, and Yellow Gate Gentleman.
idiomatic: He entered service as regular attendant, became a secretariat gentleman, and held guard general, vice director of the household guard, and yellow gate gentleman.

literal: He went out and was dismissed as General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Xiang Province.
idiomatic: He was posted out as general who pacifies the north and Xiang inspector.

literal: He became Director of the Imperial Clan.
idiomatic: He was made director of the imperial clan.

literal: He was enfeoffed as Duke of Pingle County with an open state, fief of eight hundred households.
idiomatic: He was enfeoffed duke of Pingle county, an open state, with eight hundred households.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang's reign he was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of Chariots and Cavalry, enfeoffed as Prince of Donghai, fief of one thousand households.
idiomatic: At Zhuangdi's accession he was attendant-in-ordinary and general of chariots and cavalry, enfeoffed prince of Donghai with one thousand households.

literal: Soon he was transferred to Supervisor of the Secretariat and Left Grand Master of the Household Guard, concurrently Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Soon he was secretariat supervisor and left grand master of the household guard, also right vice director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He was again appointed Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, with added Attendant-in-Ordinary.
idiomatic: He was again named grand general of chariots and cavalry with added attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: Xu had no other talent; he rose early to heavy office through kinship.
idiomatic: Xu had no other gift; kinship alone put him in high office young.

literal: When his elder brother Hao entered Luoyang, before success or defeat was settled, he was already self-satisfied in spirit, and men of the time laughed at him.
idiomatic: When his brother Hao took Luoyang, before the issue was decided Xu was already swollen with pride, and contemporaries mocked him.

literal: When Hao was defeated, he fled in hiding, was seized and sent in, and was executed in the market of the capital.
idiomatic: After Hao's fall he hid, was seized and delivered up, and beheaded in the capital market.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously given Attendant-in-Ordinary, controller of all military affairs of Yong, Hua, and Qi provinces, General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Duke, Director of the Masters of Writing, and Inspector of Yong Province.
idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne he was posthumously attendant-in-ordinary, commander of Yong, Hua, and Qi armies, general of agile cavalry, grand duke, director of the Masters of Writing, and Yong inspector.

literal: His son Yan inherited the rank.
idiomatic: His son Yan succeeded to the title.

literal: In the Wuding era he was Regular Attendant and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
idiomatic: In Wuding he was regular attendant and cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, enfeoffments were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi's founding the rank was lowered by rule.

literal: The historiographer says: The sons of Emperor Xiaowen all received instruction in the Taihe era.
idiomatic: The historiographer writes: Xiaowendi's sons were all schooled in the Taihe years.

literal: Xianyang's prestige was weighty and his rank lofty; mutual suspicion bred rebellion.
idiomatic: Xianyang's standing and rank bred suspicion and revolt.

literal: Zhao Commandery transgressed the norms of princely conduct; in the end his posthumous title was Ling.
idiomatic: Zhao Commandery overstepped princely bounds and was finally posthumously titled Ling.

literal: Guangling was long famed for keen discernment; sadly he died young—a pity.
idiomatic: Guangling had long been praised for sharp judgment; his early death was a loss.

literal: Gaoyang's talent and art were wanting, yet in the end he bore the pillar role; the Xiaochang rebellion—probably not enough to blame him.
idiomatic: Gaoyang lacked gifts, yet in the end carried the state's beam; the Xiaochang rising can scarcely be laid at his door.

literal: Beihai failed the brotherly duty of the jiju ming ode, and through luxury and debauchery destroyed himself; though calamity came through slander between kin, he also brought sorrow on himself.
idiomatic: Beihai forgot the brotherhood of the jiju ming and ruined himself in excess; though rumor between kin brought the blow, he had courted the grief himself.

literal: Hao seized power as if picking up lost objects; he perished in no time—was it lack of skill in holding it, or that heaven was about to overturn him?
idiomatic: Hao took power as easily as picking up what others dropped and was gone almost at once—was he unskilled at keeping it, or was heaven already pulling the house down?
